unit.title: Research interior decoration and design influences

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and carry out research into design influences for a new salon or spa interior.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would meet the owner and agree the brief: which area is changing, what it is used for, the budget, the time, the kind of clients and any style the owner likes. I would write down the questions my research must answer, such as which style suits the brand and which colours and materials are practical. Then I would plan my sources and a timetable. I would use secondary sources such as books, magazines and reliable websites, and primary sources such as visits to other salons, hotels or heritage buildings (with permission), my own photos, sketches and measurements, and a short interview with the owner and staff. I would record every source as I go. Next I would sort my findings into groups (colour, furniture, lighting, materials, influences), compare the ideas against the brief and budget, and present the best options to the owner.
markingPoints: Agrees the brief: purpose, budget, time, clients, style
Sets research questions and plans sources and time
Uses both secondary and primary sources, with permission for visits and photos
Records every source as the work goes on
Sorts and compares findings against the brief, then presents options

essays.stem: Explain the difference between primary and secondary sources, give two examples of each, and say how you would check that a source is reliable.
essays.modelAnswer: A primary source is information I collect myself, first hand. Examples are my own photos and sketches from a visit to a great house or a hotel lobby, measurements of a room, and an interview with a salon owner or a designer. A secondary source is information that someone else has collected and written up, such as a book on Caribbean architecture, a design magazine article or a website about Art Deco. To check that a source is reliable, I would look at who wrote it and whether they are an expert or a trusted body, such as a museum, a heritage organisation or a library book. I would check the date to see if it is up to date, and compare the facts with at least one other good source. I would be careful with websites that are selling something, or that give no author.
markingPoints: Primary: collected first hand by the researcher
Two correct primary examples (visit photos, sketches, measurements, interview)
Secondary: collected and written up by someone else, with two correct examples
Checks author or organisation and the date
Compares with another source and is careful of selling sites or no author

essays.stem: Describe the elements of design, and explain how two of them could be used in a salon reception.
essays.modelAnswer: The elements of design are the building blocks of a room. Line can be straight, curved, vertical or horizontal; vertical lines make a room feel taller and horizontal lines make it feel calm. Shape and form are the outlines and solid objects, such as a round mirror or a square desk. Colour sets the mood. Texture is how a surface feels or looks, such as rough stone or smooth glass. Pattern is a repeated design, as in tiles or fabric. Space is the area around and between things, and light, natural or artificial, shows everything else. In a salon reception, colour could be used with a calm, light neutral on the walls and the salon's brand colour on the desk front, so the brand stands out. Texture could be used with a smooth, washable desk top, a woven basket for magazines and a plant, so the space feels warm but stays easy to clean.
markingPoints: Names at least four elements: line, shape/form, colour, texture, pattern, space, light
Explains what at least three of them mean
First element applied correctly to a salon reception
Second element applied correctly to a salon reception
Links choices to practical needs (cleaning, brand, mood)

essays.stem: Explain the design principles of balance, proportion, rhythm and emphasis, giving an example of each in an interior.
essays.modelAnswer: Balance is how visual weight is spread so a room feels steady. Symmetrical balance has the same on both sides, such as a mirror with a matching lamp on each side; asymmetrical balance uses different items of equal weight, such as a large sofa balanced by two chairs and a tall plant. Proportion and scale mean that items suit each other and the size of the room: a huge chandelier in a small reception looks wrong, while a small lamp in a big hall looks lost. Rhythm is repetition that leads the eye around the room, such as the same gold frame on every station mirror, or a colour repeated in cushions and towels. Emphasis means one feature stands out as the focal point, such as a feature wall with the salon's logo behind the desk. Using these principles together makes a room look planned and comfortable.
markingPoints: Balance explained, with a symmetrical or asymmetrical example
Proportion and scale explained, with an example
Rhythm (repetition) explained, with an example
Emphasis or focal point explained, with an example
Examples are realistic for an interior or salon

essays.stem: Explain how colour schemes are built from the colour wheel, and describe the effect of warm and cool colours in a salon or spa.
essays.modelAnswer: The colour wheel shows the primary colours red, yellow and blue; the secondary colours orange, green and purple made by mixing two primaries; and the tertiary colours between them. A monochromatic scheme uses tints and shades of one colour, such as light to dark green. An analogous scheme uses colours next to each other, such as yellow, yellow-green and green, which look calm and natural. A complementary scheme uses colours opposite each other, such as blue and orange, which gives strong contrast; often one is used as the main colour and the other as an accent. A triadic scheme uses three colours evenly spaced. Warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) feel lively and cosy and seem to come towards you, so they suit a busy reception or retail area. Cool colours (blues, greens, purples) feel calm and seem to move away, so they suit a spa treatment room and make a small room look bigger.
markingPoints: Describes primary, secondary and tertiary colours on the wheel
Explains at least two schemes correctly (monochromatic, analogous, complementary, triadic)
Warm colours: lively, cosy, advancing
Cool colours: calm, receding, make a space look bigger
Applies warm and cool colours sensibly to salon or spa areas

essays.stem: Describe the main features of two historical design styles, and explain how either one could inspire a modern salon interior.
essays.modelAnswer: Georgian style, from the 1700s to the early 1800s, is based on symmetry and classical proportions. Rooms have tall sash windows, panelled walls, columns and mouldings, and fine mahogany furniture; in Jamaica it is seen in great houses and in Falmouth's old buildings. Art Deco, popular in the 1920s and 1930s, uses bold geometric shapes such as zig-zags, fans and sunbursts, shiny materials such as chrome, mirror and lacquer, and rich colours like black, gold, emerald and deep blue. A modern salon could take ideas from Art Deco without copying it fully: a fan-shaped mirror at each station, a black and gold colour scheme on the reception desk, geometric floor tiles that are still slip-resistant and washable, and brass-coloured lamps. This gives a glamorous look while the layout, lighting and materials still meet the salon's needs for safety and cleaning.
markingPoints: First style: correct period and at least two features
Second style: correct period and at least two features
Shows how one style could inspire a salon
Adapts the style rather than copying it
Keeps function and safety in mind (washable, slip-resistant, lighting)

essays.stem: Explain how Jamaica's climate, history and cultures have influenced the design of buildings and interiors here.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica is hot and humid, with strong sun, heavy rain and hurricanes. Older buildings have verandahs for shade, high ceilings and louvred (jalousie) windows to let breezes through, and light colours that reflect heat. Hip roofs and strong shutters help against storms, and builders choose materials that resist damp, mould and termites. History has left many influences. British colonial rule brought the Georgian style, seen in great houses and towns like Falmouth and Spanish Town, with symmetry and mahogany furniture, and later Victorian decoration, such as fretwork trim. African heritage shows in carving, woven baskets, bold patterns and colours, and craft traditions. Indian, Chinese, Middle Eastern and Taíno influences add fabrics, colours and motifs. Today, Jamaican designers mix these with modern ideas, using local wood, stone, art and bright tropical colours to create interiors that feel Caribbean.
markingPoints: Climate: heat, humidity, sun and storms
Design responses: verandahs, high ceilings, louvres, light colours, damp- and termite-resistant materials
British colonial influence: Georgian or Victorian features
African and other cultural influences named with examples
Modern mix of local materials, art and tropical colour

essays.stem: Describe the types of lighting used in interiors, and explain what lighting a salon needs for colour work, retail displays and a relaxing treatment room.
essays.modelAnswer: Ambient or general lighting gives the whole room an even level of light, for example ceiling panels or downlights. Task lighting is brighter light aimed at a work area, such as a lamp over a manicure table or lights around a station mirror. Accent lighting picks out a feature, such as a spotlight on artwork or products. Natural light from windows is also used, but it changes during the day and can bring glare and heat. In a salon, colour work needs bright, even, daylight-type light that shows colour well (good colour rendering), so the stylist and client see the true shade, with no strong shadows on the face. Retail displays need accent lighting to draw attention to the products. A relaxing treatment room needs soft, warm, dimmable light, placed so it does not shine into the client's eyes while she lies down, with enough task light for the therapist to work safely.
markingPoints: Ambient (general) lighting explained
Task lighting explained
Accent lighting explained, and natural light mentioned
Colour work: bright, even, daylight-type light that shows colour well
Retail: accent light; treatment room: soft, warm, dimmable, not in the eyes

essays.stem: Explain why you must record and credit your sources, and respect copyright and privacy, when you research designs.
essays.modelAnswer: Recording every source as I go (the author or organisation, title, website address, date and the date I looked at it) means I can find it again, and the salon owner or my assessor can check that my facts are true. Giving credit is honest: it shows which ideas and images came from other people and which are my own, so I am not passing off someone else's work. Copyright protects photographers, designers and writers. I can look at their work for ideas, but I must not copy a photo or a design onto a sign, advert or website without permission. I should use my own photos or images I am allowed to use. Privacy matters too: I must ask before I photograph inside someone's home or business, and I must not show people's faces or private details without their agreement.
markingPoints: Records the details of each source
Others can check the facts; the research is trustworthy
Credit is honest and avoids passing off others' work
Copyright: do not copy images or designs for use without permission
Privacy: ask before photographing homes, businesses or people

essays.stem: Describe how you would present your research findings to a salon owner, including what you would put on a mood board.
essays.modelAnswer: I would choose the two or three best ideas that fit the owner's brief and budget. For each idea I would make a mood board: a board or a screen page showing pictures of the style, a colour scheme with paint swatches, samples of fabric, flooring and finishes, examples of furniture and lighting, and a few words to describe the feeling, such as "calm tropical spa". I would add short notes beside each image to explain why I chose it and where it came from. I would also give a short written summary with the main design influences, the good and bad points of each idea, rough costs and a list of my sources. I would present it in a meeting, speaking clearly and showing the board, then ask for the owner's comments and record the decisions and any changes she wants.
markingPoints: Selects the best ideas that fit the brief and budget
Mood board: images, colour swatches, material samples, furniture and lighting
Annotations explain each choice and give its source
Short written summary: influences, pros and cons, costs, source list
Presents clearly, invites feedback and records decisions

practical1.title: Research and mood board for a salon reception in a chosen design style
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a short brief for a new reception area for a salon or hotel spa in Jamaica (who the clients are, the size of the space and a rough budget). Your group chooses one design influence to research, for example Art Deco, Georgian, Caribbean or tropical, African-inspired, Scandinavian or minimalist. Each member researches one part, using at least two sources each (one book or magazine and one website, or a primary source such as photos taken with permission): (1) the history and main features of the style; (2) colour scheme; (3) furniture and layout; (4) lighting; (5) materials and finishes, including what is washable and slip-resistant (in a group of four, parts 4 and 5 are shared). Together, make one mood board (on board or on a screen) with images, colour swatches, samples and short notes, and a source list. Each member then explains their part to the assessor in one to two minutes. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, notes and source list to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Design books and magazines, and computers or phones with internet
Board or card (about A2), scissors, glue and markers
Paint swatch cards, fabric and flooring samples or offcuts
Printer (if available) or magazines to cut up
photos: Each member's research notes with their sources written down
The colour scheme and swatches laid out
The mood board half-way, with images placed
The finished mood board with notes, close enough to read
Each member explaining their part (back or side view, unless they agree to faces)
checklist: Researched their part using at least two sources
Recorded each source correctly (title, author or website, date)
Chose images and samples that fit the style and the brief
Wrote clear notes explaining the choices
Considered function and safety (washable, slip-resistant, lighting)
Explained their part clearly to the assessor
Shared the work and helped the group finish on time
safety: Use scissors and craft knives carefully, cutting away from the body
Use glue in a ventilated room and keep it away from eyes
Keep cables from computers and printers out of walkways
Use only images you are allowed to use, and credit every source

practical2.title: Survey of an interior and a design-influence comparison poster
practical2.brief: Your group surveys an interior at the Centre, such as the salon, reception or a classroom, or uses a photo pack of a Jamaican heritage building given by the assessor. Each member records one part of the interior with a sketch and photos: (1) a floor plan with measurements; (2) colours and materials; (3) furniture and fittings; (4) lighting and windows; (5) decoration and details (in a group of four, parts 4 and 5 are shared). Then, as a group, compare the interior with one design influence you research (for example Georgian, Victorian, Art Deco, Caribbean vernacular or minimalist), and make a poster that shows: what you found; which design influences you can see; a short timeline of the style you researched; the elements and principles of design at work; two ideas to improve the space; and a source list. Each member presents their part of the poster. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, sketches and poster to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Clipboards, squared paper, pencils and rulers
A phone or camera for photos (with permission)
photos: Each member's sketch or photo of their part of the interior
The research notes on the chosen design influence
The finished poster, close enough to read
checklist: Measured and recorded their part of the interior accurately
Named design elements and principles correctly
Researched the design influence using reliable, recorded sources
Made a fair comparison between the interior and the style
Worked well with the group and kept to time
safety: Ask permission before entering or photographing any room, and do not photograph people without consent
Do not climb on furniture to measure; use a checked step stool if needed, with someone holding it
Keep walkways and fire exits clear while you work
Work in pairs if you leave the classroom
